reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants and toddlers, typically ileocolic, when one bowel segment telescopes into the adjacent distal segment
Classically presents with sudden intermittent colicky pain and drawing up of the legs, alternating with quiet or lethargic intervals
The late triad of colicky pain, a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass, and redcurrant-jelly stool is characteristic but incomplete in many children
Most cases in infants are idiopathic, often following a viral illness with lymphoid (Peyer patch) hypertrophy acting as the lead point
Ultrasound is the investigation of choice, showing the target/doughnut sign in transverse section and a pseudokidney sign longitudinally
Non-operative reduction by air or hydrostatic (contrast) enema is first-line in the stable child without peritonitis or perforation
A pathological lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, polyp, or lymphoma is more likely in older children and in recurrent cases
reference.pathophysiology: Intussusception occurs when a proximal segment of bowel (the intussusceptum) invaginates into the lumen of the contiguous distal segment (the intussuscipiens), dragging its mesentery with it. The commonest ileocolic form is usually idiopathic, frequently preceded by a viral infection that causes hypertrophy of ileal lymphoid tissue serving as a lead point. Progressive telescoping compresses the mesenteric vessels, producing venous congestion, mucosal oedema, and bleeding that gives rise to the redcurrant-jelly stool; if unrelieved, arterial compromise leads to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. In older children an anatomical lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst, polyp, or tumour is more often responsible.
additionalDifferentials: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (which can also trigger intussusception)
Constipation or colic in an unsettled infant
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound for target and pseudokidney signs and to seek a lead point
Abdominal radiograph to assess for obstruction or free air before reduction
Air or contrast enema, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic for reduction
Basic bloods and hydration assessment to guide resuscitation
Evaluation for a pathological lead point in older or recurrent cases
Post-reduction observation and repeat imaging if symptoms recur
redFlags: Peritonitis, abdominal rigidity, or signs of perforation contraindicating enema reduction
Marked lethargy or shock, which may be the presenting feature and mimic neurological illness
Prolonged symptoms with signs of bowel ischaemia
Recurrent intussusception suggesting a pathological lead point requiring surgery
reference.prognosis: Early diagnosis with prompt enema reduction resolves most idiopathic cases with excellent outcomes, though a minority recur. Delayed presentation with ischaemic or necrotic bowel requires operative reduction or resection and carries higher morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing lethargy or altered consciousness to a neurological cause and missing intussusception
Waiting for the full classic triad, which delays diagnosis and reduction
Attempting enema reduction in the presence of peritonitis or perforation
Failing to consider a pathological lead point in older children and recurrent cases
Under-resuscitating a dehydrated child before attempting reduction
management: Resuscitate with intravenous fluids and electrolyte correction, and decompress with a nasogastric tube if the bowel is obstructed
Undertake image-guided non-operative reduction by air (pneumatic) or hydrostatic contrast enema as first-line therapy in the stable child without peritonitis or perforation
Proceed to operative reduction, and resection of non-viable bowel, when enema reduction fails or where there is peritonitis, perforation or established ischaemia
Give peri-procedural broad-spectrum antibiotics and adequate analgesia when perforation or ischaemic bowel is suspected
Seek and treat an anatomical lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst or polyp in older children and recurrent cases
Observe after reduction for early recurrence and repeat imaging if symptoms recur
Refer to paediatric surgery and manage in a centre equipped for both radiological reduction and operative intervention
